titleEn: The Song of the Cid — The Cid's escort and Avengalvón meet the ladies at Medinaceli (tirada 83, second part, lines 1453–1526)
part: Tirada 83 (second part) · The Cid's escort and Avengalvón meet the ladies at Medinaceli (lines 1453–1526)

sentences.i: Now I will tell you of the knights who carried the message. In the hour that my Çid of Vivar learned of it, it pleased him to the heart and he grew glad again; and from his lips he began to speak:
sentences.n: Tirada 83 (continued; assonance á) — Pedro Vermúdez sets out from Valencia to meet Ximena; at Molina Avengalvón joins him; they find Minaya at Medinaceli (the second half of Pidal's rubric: Pedro Vermúdez parte de Valencia para recibir a Jimena. En Molina se le une Avengalvón. Encuentran a Minaya en Medinaceli). The assonance runs on from part 83a: stressed á at the line-end (Bivar, alegrar, fablar, sperar), with á-e endings counted alongside (menssaje, Fáñez, grandes, faze). Direvos = vos diré, 'I will tell you': the future with the pronoun fastened after it, as the verb opens the line; the minstrel turns from Minaya at Medinaceli back to the three knights sent to Valencia at vv. 1405–06. levaron = llevaron. al ora que, 'at the hour when' (ora = hora). sopo = supo, preterite of saber. plógol = plógole, 'it pleased him', preterite of plazer with le squeezed to -l. de coraçon, 'from the heart'. tornós a alegrar = tornóse a alegrar, 'he turned to gladness', grew glad again. de la su boca, article + possessive, the epic formula for speech; conpeçó de fablar = comenzó a hablar (f- for h-).

sentences.t: “Qui buen mandadero enbía, tal deve sperar.
sentences.l: “Who good messenger sends, such he-must expect.
sentences.i: “Whoever sends a good messenger should look for the like in return.
sentences.n: A proverb. qui = quien, 'whoever'. mandadero, 'messenger' (mandado, 'message'). enbía = envía. tal, 'such', read as 'such (an answer)', the good news that comes back with a good messenger: Minaya has done what he was sent to do. sperar = esperar, with the e- dropped. deve, 'must, ought to' (= debe). The exact point of tal is not certain; Pidal gives no note.

sentences.t:
Tú, Muño Gustioz e Per Vermu[doz] delant,
e Martín Antolínez, un Burgalés leal,
el obispo don Jero[me], coronado de prestar,
cavalguedes con çiento guisados pora huebos de lidiar;
sentences.l:
You, Muño Gustioz and Per Vermu[doz] ahead,
and Martín Antolínez, a Burgalés loyal,
the bishop don Jero[me], tonsured-one of worth,
you-may-ride with a-hundred equipped for need of fighting;
sentences.i: You, Muño Gustioz, and you, Per Vermudoz, at the head, and Martín Antolínez, a loyal man of Burgos, and the bishop Don Jerome, a churchman of worth: ride out with a hundred men equipped as for battle;
sentences.n: Tú, singular, addresses the first name, then the list grows and the verb turns plural, cavalguedes, present subjunctive 2nd pl. of cavalgar used as a command, 'ride!' Vermu[doz] and Jero[me]: the endings are Pidal's (in italics). delant, 'ahead, in front': Per Vermudoz, the Çid's standard-bearer, is to lead (Pidal's rubric names him alone as setting out); the word also fills the assonance. Burgalés, 'man of Burgos'. coronado, 'tonsured', a cleric (the crown-shaped tonsure); de prestar, 'of worth' (v. 1432). don Jerome is the cleric who came 'from the East' and was made bishop of Valencia (vv. 1288–1303). guisados, 'equipped, made ready' (past participle of guisar, used as a noun). Pidal's note to v. 1461: pora huebos de lidiar, 'para las necesidades de lidiar', 'for the needs of fighting', 'como para lid', 'as for battle'; the same at v. 1695 (compare vv. 1374 and 123). huebos, 'need', from Latin opus.

sentences.t:
por Santa María vos vayades passar,
vayades a Molina, que iaze más adelant,
tiénela Ave[n]galvón, mio amigo es de paz,
con otros çiento cavalleros bien vos conssigrá;
sentences.l:
by Santa María yourselves you-are-to-go to-pass,
you-are-to-go to Molina, which lies more ahead,
holds-it Ave[n]galvón, my friend he-is of peace,
with other hundred knights well you he-will-escort;
sentences.i: go by way of Santa María, and on to Molina, which lies farther on: Avengalvón holds it, my friend at peace with me; with another hundred knights he will escort you well;
sentences.n: Pidal's note to v. 1462: Santa María, today Albarracín, in the province of Teruel; the Arab writers call it Santa María of the East of al-Andalus (to tell it from the one in the West, the Algarve in Portugal), or Santa María de Aben Razín (Santa María d'Alvarazín, v. 2645), 'porque la poseía desde antiguo la familia musulmana de los Aben Razín, que ahora era tributaria del Cid', 'because the Muslim family of the Aben Razín had held it from of old, and was now tributary to the Çid'. vayades, present subjunctive 2nd pl. of ir (= vayáis), a command again; vos vayades passar, 'go on your way and pass (by it)': ir with the reflexive vos and a bare infinitive. iaze = yace, 'lies'. tiénela = la tiene. Ave[n]galvón, the Moorish lord of Molina (the n is Pidal's, in italics, as again below). mio amigo es de paz, 'he is my friend in peace', a Moorish ally bound to the Çid. conssigrá, 'he will accompany, escort', read as a contracted future of conseguir, 'to follow, keep company with' (= conseguirá); Pidal gives no note on the form.

sentences.t:
id pora Medina quanto lo pudiéredes far,
mi mugier e mis fijas con Minaya Albar Fáñez,
así commo a mí dixieron, hi los podredes fallar;
con grand ondra aduzídmelas delant.
sentences.l:
go to Medina as-much-as it you-shall-be-able to-do,
my wife and my daughters with Minaya Albar Fáñez,
so as to me they-said, there them you-will-be-able to-find;
with great honor bring-me-them before.
sentences.i: go to Medinaceli as fast as ever you can: my wife and my daughters, with Minaya Álvar Fáñez, you will find there, as I have been told; bring them to me with great honour.
sentences.n: id, imperative 2nd pl. of ir. quanto lo pudiéredes far, 'as much as you can do it', as fast as you are able: pudiéredes, future subjunctive 2nd pl. of poder; far, short form of fazer. Medina is Medinaceli, the farthest limit of Alfonso's realm (Pidal's note to v. 1382). The wife and daughters are named first and taken up by los, masculine because the company includes Minaya. a mí dixieron = me dijeron: the three knights' message of vv. 1406–12. hi = allí, 'there'. podredes = podréis; fallar = hallar (f- for h-). aduzídmelas = aducídmelas, imperative of aduzir, 'to bring', with me and las both fastened on; delant, 'before me'.

sentences.i: And I shall stay in Valencia, which has cost me dear; it would be great folly if I were to leave it unguarded; I shall stay in Valencia, for I hold it as my own.”
sentences.n: fincaré, future of fincar, 'to stay, remain'; ffincaré, the f doubled, a spelling only. costadom ha = costado me ha, 'it has cost me', the pronoun squeezed to -m onto the participle, which stands before its auxiliary. seríe, conditional of ser (= sería), printed so in Pidal, with the accent on the i, where elsewhere he prints serié (vv. 1403, 519); followed as printed, read as serié. desenparás, 'I abandoned, left unprotected', imperfect subjunctive 1st sg. of desenparar (= desamparase), the final -e of desenparasse dropped. heredad, 'heritage, land held by right' (v. 1401). The repeated yo fincaré frames the thought: the Çid will not leave his conquest.

sentences.t:
Esto era dicho, pienssan de cavalgar,
e quanto que pueden non fincan de andar.
sentences.l:
This was said, they-think of to-ride,
and as-much as they-can not they-stop of going.
sentences.i: No sooner was it said than they set out to ride, and as hard as they can they never cease from travelling.
sentences.n: Esto era dicho, 'this was said', the moment the order was given. pienssan de cavalgar, pensar de + infinitive, 'set about riding'. quanto que pueden, 'as much as they can'. non fincan de andar, 'they do not stop going', fincar de, 'to leave off'; andar, 'to travel, go on'.

sentences.t:
Troçieron a Santa María e vinieron albergar a Fron[chales],
e el otro día viniéron a Molina posar.
sentences.l:
They-passed to Santa María and came to-lodge at Fron[chales],
and the other day came to Molina to-lodge.
sentences.i: They passed Santa María and came to lodge at Bronchales, and the next day they came to Molina to rest.
sentences.n: Troçieron, preterite of troçir, 'to pass, go by'. vinieron albergar, venir + bare infinitive, 'came to lodge'. Pidal's note to v. 1475: Fronchales, today Bronchales (25 kilometres from Albarracín), a village of the province of Teruel on the border of Guadalajara; from Bronchales to Molina is 45 kilometres, and it is a day's journey, as the next line says (for distances covered on other days, see v. 2877). -chales is Pidal's restoration (in italics). el otro día, 'the next day'. viniéron is printed with an acute on the e, probably a misprint (vinieron in the line above): read as vinieron. posar, 'to lodge, halt'.

sentences.t:
El moro Ave[n]galvón, quando sopo el menssaje,
saliólos reçebir con grant gozo que faze:
sentences.l:
The Moor Ave[n]galvón, when he-learned the message,
went-out-them to-receive with great joy that he-makes:
sentences.i: The Moor Avengalvón, when he learned the message, came out to receive them with a great show of joy:
sentences.n: El moro, 'the Moor': the poem's word for the Muslim lords of al-Andalus, here a friend. saliólos reçebir = salió a recibirlos: the pronoun of the infinitive climbs onto the main verb, and salir takes the bare infinitive. con grant gozo que faze, 'with great joy that he makes', with a great show of gladness; faze = hace, present amid the preterites, the usual epic tense-mixing.

sentences.t:
“¿Venides, los vassallos de myo amigo natural?
A mí non me pesa, sabet, mucho me plaze!”
sentences.l:
“Come-you, the vassals of my friend natural?
To me not it weighs, know-ye, much to-me it-pleases!”
sentences.i: “Are you come, vassals of my true friend? It does not grieve me — be sure of it — it pleases me greatly!”
sentences.n: Venides = venís, 2nd pl. of venir, a greeting in the form of a question. myo, spelled with y here, as printed. amigo natural, 'friend by nature', a true and bound friend (natural, 'by birth, rightful', as in señor natural). non me pesa … mucho me plaze, the same thing said twice, negatively and then positively, an emphatic courtesy. sabet = sabed, 'know it'.

sentences.i: Muño Gustioz spoke, waiting for no one: “My Çid sends you his greeting, and charged us to ask this of you: that with a hundred knights you come quickly to his aid;
sentences.n: non speró a nadi, 'waited for no one', spoke up at once; speró = esperó; nadi = nadie. saludava, imperfect, 'was greeting', the tense of a message carried from far off: 'sends greeting'. mandólo recabdar, 'he ordered it to be seen to', lo pointing forward to the que-clause; recabdar, 'to accomplish, carry through'. privádol = privado le: privado, 'quickly', an adverb, with le, 'him', squeezed on. acorrades, present subjunctive 2nd pl. of acorrer, 'to help, succour'. co[n], the n Pidal's (in italics). The joining of the clauses is loose, as in speech.

sentences.i: his wife and daughters are at Medinaceli; go for them, bring them here to him, and do not part from them until you reach Valencia.”
sentences.n: que vayades …, que adugades …, the que-clauses still hang on the Çid's charge. adugades, present subjunctive 2nd pl. of aduzir, 'to bring'. gelas = ge + las, 'them to him' (ge is le before lo, la; modern se las). acá, 'hither', to Valencia, where the speaker belongs. ffata = fasta = hasta, the f doubled, a spelling. dellas = de ellas. partades, present subjunctive of partir, 'to part', with vos, 'yourselves'.

sentences.t: Dixo Ave[n]galvón: “fer lo he de veluntad.”
sentences.l: Said Ave[n]galvón: “do it I-have of will.”
sentences.i: Avengalvón said: “I will do it gladly.”
sentences.n: fer lo he = lo haré, the split future, infinitive + he with the pronoun between; de veluntad = de voluntad, 'willingly'. Word for word Minaya's answer to the abbot at v. 1447.

sentences.i: That night he gave them a great feast; in the morning they set out to ride. They had asked him for a hundred; but he goes with two hundred.
sentences.n: noch = noche, the final -e dropped. conducho, 'provisions, fare' (v. 1409), here a lavish supper; grand set at the end for the assonance. a la mañana, 'in the morning'. çientol = çiento le, 'a hundred of him', the le squeezed onto the number: they asked him for a hundred knights (v. 1483). pidieron, preterite, beside the present va: the tense-mixing again. Avengalvón doubles what was asked.

sentences.t:
Passan las montañas, que son fieras e grandes,
passaron [desí] Mata de T[a]ranz
de tal guisa que ningún miedo non han,
por el val de Arbux[ue]lo pienssan a deprunar.
sentences.l:
They-pass the mountains, which are wild and great,
they-passed [then] Mata of T[a]ranz
of such manner that no fear not they-have,
through the vale of Arbux[ue]lo they-think to descend.
sentences.i: They cross the mountains, which are wild and high; then they crossed the Mata de Taranz in such a way that they have no fear at all, and set about going down the valley of Arbujuelo.
sentences.n: Pidal's note to v. 1491: las montañas are those he later calls montes de Luzón (v. 2653); Luzón is a village of the province of Guadalajara, between Medinaceli and Molina, and the oak and pine woods that once covered that land are, he says, much diminished today. fieras, 'wild, great'. [desí], 'then, next', Pidal's restoration (in italics), as is the a of T[a]ranz. Pidal's note to v. 1492: the Mata de Taranz, which the poem elsewhere calls campo de Taranz (v. 1544), is today called 'campo Taranz', 'una llanura pedregosa que se dilata sobre el alto del valle de Arbujuelo', 'a stony plain that stretches over the head of the valley of Arbujuelo', between the provinces of Soria and Guadalajara. Pidal numbers the line de tal guisa … 1492b (the label is printed in his margin), keeping the traditional count. de tal guisa que, 'in such a way that'; ningún miedo non han, the double negative. Pidal's note to v. 1493: val de Arbux[ue]lo (the ue his), today the valle de Arbujuelo, a stream feeding the Jalón; small as it is, it is named whenever the poem's characters travel between Valencia and Castile (vv. 1543, 2656). pienssan a deprunar, 'set about descending' (pensar a, a variant of pensar de); deprunar, 'to go down', a rare word.

sentences.i: And at Medinaceli every precaution is taken. Minaya Álvar Fáñez saw them coming armed and was afraid; he sent two knights to learn the truth of it. They make no delay, for they have it at heart;
sentences.n: Pidal's note to v. 1494: todo el recabdo está, 'hay toda clase de precauciones', 'every kind of precaution is taken'; the poet stresses the care Minaya takes to make the ladies' journey safe (compare vv. 1511, 1567); 'desde Medina se divisa todo el valle de Arbujuelo, y al ver por él venir gente de armas, Minaya envía a saber quiénes son', 'from Medina the whole valley of Arbujuelo can be seen, and on seeing armed men coming along it, Minaya sends to find out who they are'. The whole of v. 1494b is in italics in Pidal's print: it is his restoration. He prints no number beside it: the label 1494b is this edition's provisional letter after the preceding line, not Pidal's. vídolos = viólos, 'he saw them'; temiós = temióse, 'he feared', two verbs set side by side with no and between. Alvar, unaccented, as printed (in italic type the accent cannot be made out for certain). sopiesse[n], imperfect subjunctive 3rd pl. of saber (= supiesen), 'that they might learn'; the n is Pidal's, as is the n of detarda[n], 'they delay'. de coraçon lo han, 'they have it at heart', they do it with a will (aver = 'have').

sentences.t:
el uno fincó con ellos y el otro tornó a Albar Fáñez:
“Virtos del Campeador a nos vienen buscar;
sentences.l:
the one stayed with them and the other returned to Albar Fáñez:
“Forces of-the Campeador to us come to-seek;
sentences.i: one stayed with them and the other went back to Álvar Fáñez: “It is the Campeador's men coming to look for us;
sentences.n: el uno … el otro, 'the one … the other' of the two knights. fincó, preterite of fincar, 'stayed'. y = e, 'and'. Virtos, 'forces, troops', as at v. 657 (creçen estos virtos): a rare word, perhaps from Latin virtus, 'strength'; the sense is clear from the context, the form less so. a nos vienen buscar, 'come to seek us', venir + bare infinitive; a nos, 'us', the pronoun set before the verb.

sentences.t:
afevos aquí Per Vermu[doz delant]
e Muño Gustioz que vos quieren sin hart,
e Martin Antolínez, el Burgalés natural,
e obispo don Jero[me], coranado leal,
sentences.l:
behold-you here Per Vermu[doz ahead]
and Muño Gustioz who you love without guile,
and Martin Antolínez, the Burgalés native,
and bishop don Jero[me], tonsured-one loyal,
sentences.i: here, look, is Per Vermudoz at the head, and Muño Gustioz, who are your friends without guile, and Martín Antolínez, the true man of Burgos, and the bishop Don Jerome, a loyal churchman,
sentences.n: afevos, 'behold', the presentative afé + vos (v. 1431). doz delant are Pidal's (in italics); the next line he numbers 1499b. que vos quieren, 'who love you', plural for the pair. sin hart = sin arte, 'without guile, trick or flaw' (the same word as hart at v. 1204, where Pidal's note reads it as art: sin art 'without deceit', and then 'perfectly'). Martin, unaccented here, as printed. el Burgalés natural, 'the native of Burgos', natural 'by birth'. Pidal's note to v. 1501: coranado (as at v. 1993), a form found alongside coronado (vv. 1288, 1460, etc.), 'clérigo', 'cleric'. The list mirrors the Çid's own at vv. 1458–60.

sentences.i: and the governor Avengalvón with the forces he brings, out of love for my Çid, to do him great honour; they are all coming together, and will be here at any moment.”
sentences.n: Pidal's note to v. 1502: alcáyaz, 'alcaide', 'el que tiene a su cargo una fortaleza', 'the one who has a fortress in his charge'; Avengalvón governed Molina (vv. 1464, 1545). su[e]s = sus, an old possessive plural, the e Pidal's (in italics). trahe = trae. por sabor de mio Çid, 'for the pleasure of my Çid', for love of him. de grand óndral dar = de grand ondra le dar, 'to give him great honour', le squeezed onto ondra; read here with le = the Çid (it could refer to Minaya's party); the construction is loose. óndral is printed with an acute on the o, followed as printed. en uno, 'together, as one'. agora = ahora; llegarán, future of llegar.

sentences.t:
Essora dixo Minaya: “vay[a]mos cavalgar.”
Esso ff[o] apriessa fecho, que nos quieren detardar.
sentences.l:
Then said Minaya: “let-us-go to-ride.”
That w[as] swiftly done, for not-themselves they-want to-delay.
sentences.i: Then Minaya said: “Let us mount and ride.” That was quickly done, for they have no wish to delay.
sentences.n: Essora = entonces, 'then' (ess' ora, 'that hour'). vay[a]mos cavalgar, 'let us go ride', present subjunctive of ir + bare infinitive; the second a is Pidal's. ff[o] = fue, the o Pidal's (in italics). apriessa = aprisa, 'quickly'. nos = non se, 'not themselves', squeezed into one: que nos quieren detardar, 'for they do not wish to delay'. In Pidal's print the margin number 1505 stands beside Esso ffo, which by count is 1506; his labels 1500 and 1510 and his note to v. 1509 fix the numbering used here.

sentences.t:
Bien salieron den çiento que non pareçen mal,
en buenos cavallos a cuberturas de çendales
e peytrales a cascaviellos, e escudos a los cuellos [traen],
e en las manos lanças que pendones traen,
sentences.l:
Well went-out thence a-hundred who not look bad,
on good horses with trappings of sendals
and breast-straps with little-bells, and shields at the necks [they-bring],
and in the hands lances which pennons bear,
sentences.i: Fully a hundred rode out from there, and they made no poor show, on good horses with trappings of silk and breast-straps hung with bells, carrying their shields at their necks and in their hands lances that bear pennons,
sentences.n: Bien … den çiento, 'fully a hundred … from there': den = de + ende, 'thence', from Medinaceli (a partitive 'of them' is also possible). que non pareçen mal, 'who do not look poor', a fine show (pareçer = parecer). cuberturas, 'coverings, trappings' for the horses; çendales, 'sendal', a light silk. peytrales, 'breast-straps' of the harness; a cascaviellos, 'with little bells' (= cascabeles). Pidal's note to v. 1509: 'antiguamente se adornaban los petrales de los caballos con grandes cascabeles, especialmente para correr en las fiestas', 'in former times horses' breast-straps were adorned with large bells, especially for running in festivities'; on the shield at the neck he refers to p. 105 of his introduction, where the shield is carried hung at the neck by a strap (tiracol o correa), and gripped against the heart, still hanging there, to charge. [traen], 'they carry', is Pidal's restoration (in italics). que pendones traen, 'which bear pennons'.

sentences.t:
que sopiessen los otros de qué seso era Álbar Fáñez
o qu[o]mo saliera de Castiella con estas dueñas que trahe.
sentences.l:
that might-know the others of what sense was Álbar Fáñez
or h[o]w he-had-come-out of Castiella with these ladies that he-brings.
sentences.i: so that the others should know what good judgement Álvar Fáñez had, and in what style he had come out of Castile with these ladies he is bringing.
sentences.n: que sopiessen, 'so that (the others) might know', purpose (sopiessen = supiesen). seso, 'sense, judgement'. qu[o]mo = commo, 'how', the o Pidal's (in italics). saliera, 'had come out', the -ra form in its old pluperfect sense (= había salido). trahe = trae, present after the past: the tense-mixing. Castiella = Castilla.

sentences.i: Those who were scouting ahead and arriving first at once take up arms and begin to sport with them; near the Jalón great is the rejoicing as they ride.
sentences.n: Pidal's note to v. 1513: mesurar means 'explorar, reconocer el terreno', 'to explore, reconnoitre the ground'; it refers to the scouts of the cavalry of Pero Vermúdez and Avengalvón. ivan mesurando e llegando, ir + gerund, 'were going along scouting and arriving'. luego, 'at once'. Pidal's note to v. 1514: tómanse a deportar, 'comienzan a deportarse', 'they begin to disport themselves'; deportarse, 'solazarse con ejercicios corporales', 'to take one's pleasure in bodily exercises': the mock combat of a festive welcome. Salón is the river Jalón, which runs below Medinaceli. tan grandes gozos van, 'such great joys go', such rejoicing there is along the way, with no que-clause to follow.

sentences.t: Don llegan los otros, a Minaya se van homillar.
sentences.l: Where arrive the others, to Minaya themselves they-go to-humble.
sentences.i: When the rest come up, they go to make their bow to Minaya.
sentences.n: Don = donde, used of time, 'when, where'. los otros, 'the others', the main body behind the scouts. se van homillar, 'go to humble themselves', to bow in greeting (omillar, compare Omillom, v. 1396); ir + bare infinitive.

sentences.t:
Quando llegó Ave[n]galvón, dont a ojo [lo] ha,
sonrrisándose de la boca, hivalo abraçar,
en el ombro lo saluda, ca tal es [so] husaje:
sentences.l:
When arrived Ave[n]galvón, when in eye [him] he-has,
smiling-himself from the mouth, he-went-him to-embrace,
on the shoulder him he-greets, for such is [his] custom:
sentences.i: When Avengalvón came up and had him in sight, he went, smiling, to embrace him, and greets him with a kiss on the shoulder, for such is his custom:
sentences.n: dont a ojo [lo] ha, 'when he has him in sight': dont = donde, here 'when, as soon as'; a ojo aver, 'to have in eye'; [lo] is Pidal's restoration (in italics). sonrrisándose de la boca, 'smiling with his mouth', a stock formula (compare v. 1527). hivalo abraçar = ívalo abrazar, 'he went to embrace him', iva (imperfect of ir) with lo fastened on, and the bare infinitive; the h is a spelling only. Pidal's note to v. 1519: 'le besa en el hombro', 'he kisses him on the shoulder' (compare v. 3030 for saludar, 'to kiss'); 'era costumbre propia de los moros saludar besando en el hombro, en el brazo (así Boabdil al rey Católico cuando le entregó Granada) o en el cuello (así en Roland, 601)', 'it was the Moors' own custom to greet by kissing on the shoulder, on the arm (so Boabdil did to the Catholic King when he surrendered Granada) or on the neck (so in the Roland, 601)'. [so] husaje = su usaje, 'his custom'; so is Pidal's (in italics), and the h is a spelling only.

sentences.i: “A good day to you, Minaya Álvar Fáñez! You bring these ladies through whom we shall all be the greater: the wife of the fighting Çid and his own daughters.
sentences.n: Tan buen día convusco, 'so good a day with you', a greeting; convusco = con vos, the old fused form. Traedes = traéis. por o valdremos más, 'by which we shall be worth more', o = donde, 'whereby, through whom'; valdremos, future of valer: the honour done the Çid's ladies will raise the honour of all who serve them. lidiador, 'fighter, warrior', the Çid's epithet. ffijas naturales, 'his daughters by birth', his own daughters; ffijas, the f doubled, a spelling.

sentences.t:
ondrar vos hemos todos, ca tal es la su auze,
maguer que mal le queramos, non gelo podremos f[ar],
sentences.l:
honor you we-have all, for such is the his fortune,
although that ill to-him we-may-wish, not it-to-him we-shall-be-able to-d[o],
sentences.i: We shall all do you honour, for such is his fortune that, even if we wished him ill, we could not do it,
sentences.n: ondrar vos hemos = os honraremos, 'we shall honour you', the split future, infinitive + hemos with the pronoun between. Pidal's note to v. 1523: auze, 'ventura, dicha', 'fortune, good luck' (v. 2366); la su auze, article + possessive. maguer que, 'although, even if', with the present subjunctive queramos, 'we may wish'. mal le queramos, 'we may wish him ill'. non gelo podremos f[ar] = no se lo podremos hacer, 'we could not do it to him', gelo = ge (le) + lo, the ill wished; f[ar], the ending Pidal's (in italics). The Moor's courtesy is frank: the Çid's luck makes him unassailable.

sentences.t:
en paz o en guerra de lo nuestro abrá;
muchol tengo por torpe qui non conosçe la verdad.”
sentences.l:
in peace or in war of the ours he-will-have;
much-him I-hold for dull who not knows the truth.”
sentences.i: in peace or in war he shall have of what is ours; I hold him a very dullard who does not recognise the truth.”
sentences.n: de lo nuestro abrá, 'he will have of what is ours', a partitive de: whether in peace as tribute or in war as booty, the Çid will take a share of the Moors' wealth. abrá = habrá, future of aver. muchol = mucho le: tener por, 'to hold as', le anticipating qui …, 'him who …'. torpe, 'dull, slow-witted'. qui = quien. conosçe = conoce, 'recognizes'. Here tirada 83 ends; Minaya's answer opens tirada 84 in a new assonance (á-a).
